title: Asking the Mud to Bring Her Home
hookLine: a lotus pond drained in summer, all mud, and a hymn that asks the mud itself to bring the goddess home
carry: the lotus: fortune rising clean from the mud
tomorrow: what does a hymn of a thousand names call the goddess first?
last: TRUTH OF SPEECH, COUNTED AS RICHES.

cards: Drain a lotus pond in the dry season and you don't find anything pretty. You find mud, thick and dark, with old roots running through it like cables. But that's where the flower lives.

Every bloom draws on what's down there in the dark. The Sri Sukta has been calling the lotus goddess all week. And when it finally asks her to move in for good, it doesn't ask the flower to do the inviting.

teach.b: Here's the line, in paraphrase. Through Kardama she has children. Kardama, come and dwell with me.
Make Sri, the mother garlanded with lotuses, dwell in my family. Kardama is a name, and as a word it means mud. Tradition hears him as her son.
So the singer asks her own child to move in, so his mother will follow. The next line does the same with water.

In paraphrase: may the waters bring forth soft and gentle things. Chiklita, live in my house, and make the divine mother Sri dwell in my family. Chiklita, tradition says, is another of her children, linked to moisture.
Mud and water: the two humble things a lotus can't live without. He doesn't ask the gold or the elephants to bring her, but the plainest, dampest parts of the earth.

And this is why Lakshmi is called Padma and Kamala, both names for the lotus, and why she's pictured seated on one. Hindus love the lotus for what it does: it roots in mud and rises clean, water sliding off its leaves.
Many teachers read it as a picture of a good life: grown out of ordinary, messy ground, and not stained by it.

teach.h: THE LOTUS RISES CLEAN FROM THE MUD.
teach.b: Not my house only, but my people, across generations, some readers say.
That's this week: a guest welcomed, a goddess who fills others, I choose you, a vow's heat, Alakshmi shown the door, riches wider than money, and now the mud.
The hymn goes on a little further, but this is where the path leaves it. Tomorrow, a different hymn, one that praises the goddess by her names.

how: Some Hindus chant the whole Sri Sukta at home or in temples during Lakshmi worship, at Diwali and on other days, often while offering lotus flowers, lamps and sweets.

o: a hymn about draining ponds before the rains
a prayer to keep mud and dirt out of a house
a hymn asking even the mud to bring Sri home

games.q: asking her to stay — tap the pairs.
p: linked to moisture, asked to live here

s: the singer asks the elephants to bring her home
he asks Kardama, the mud, and Chiklita, linked to the waters.
tradition hears Kardama as her son
so the singer invites her child, hoping the mother will follow.
the hymn asks her to stay only for one season
it asks her to dwell in the singer's family, across the line.

games.q: you want the lotus goddess to come and live in your family for good. whom do you ask to bring her?
o: a king, with gold and elephants.
Kardama, her son, whose name means mud.
the brightest star in the sky.
games.why: the hymn asks Kardama, the mud, to dwell with the singer, so that Sri will dwell in the family; then Chiklita and the waters. the lotus is invited through what it grows from.

practice: Bring to mind something plain that holds your life up: a hard season you came through, a parent's ordinary work, the early mornings.

Then notice what has grown out of it that you're glad of now, and rest with the two together, root and flower. If you pray, you can thank the goddess, or God, for both; if you don't, let the plain thing be honored for once.

wordCard.voice: The Sri Sukta. The hymn that calls Sri near, chooses her, and finally asks Kardama, the mud, to bring the lotus mother home to stay.

orig.note: Sanskrit: kardama, mud, and in the Sri Sukta a name, heard by tradition as Sri's son.

carryVoice: Your line: the lotus, fortune rising clean from the mud. Mud and water, asked to bring her home. Go gently.

sources.ref: Sri Sukta, verses 11–12 (Rig Veda khila, as commonly recited)
